list.listitem: Active management of the third stage of labor is superior to expectant management for reducing postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) with an NNT of 12; obstetric care facilities should have guidelines for routine administration of uterotonics. A
Oxytocin is recommended consistently across national guidelines for PPH prevention in vaginal deliveries. A
Clinical estimation of blood loss is unreliable. C
Uterotonics should be the first-line medical treatment in patients who have persistent hemorrhage after initial massage. A

Routine use of tranexamic acid to prevent PPH is not warranted. A When used as treament, tranexamic acid should be considered when initial medical therapy fails, and initiated as soon as possible for greatest benefit. B

background.definition: The World Health Organization defines primary postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) as blood loss of 500 mL or more in the first 24 hours postpartum. ACOG defines primary PPH as blood loss of 1000 mL or more accompanied by signs or symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours, regardless of birth process, and secondary PPH as excessive bleeding that occurs from 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum.

list.listitem: The incidence of PPH is 4% to 11% of pregnancies. The true incidence is difficult to discern as blood loss is difficult to accurately assess; trials of uterotonics often report higher rates of PPH than cited here.
In a World Health Organization (WHO) 28 country survey, the vast majority (95.3%) used uterotonic prophylaxis and the reported rate of PPH was 1.2%.

PPH requiring massive transfusion, defined as ≥8 units of red blood cells within 24 hours of giving birth, occurs in 23/100,000 deliveries (95% confidence interval [CI], 19-26) annually, based on the UK Obstetric Surveillance System.
PPH is the most frequent cause (approximately 25%) of maternal mortality worldwide.
There is approximately 1 death in every 1000 deliveries in developing countries.
There is approximately 1 death in every 100,000 deliveries in developed countries.

Peripartum hysterectomy occurs in 0.7/1000 deliveries in wealthier countries, with uterine atony (27%) being the second most common reason after placental pathology (38%). In a population-based French study, hysterectomy was performed in 72/6660 women with PPH (1.1%, 95% CI 0.8-1.4%) and in 0.05% of deliveries (95% CI 0.04-0.06).
Uterine atony (70%-80%).
Trauma (20%).
Retained placental products (10%).
Coagulation defects (1%).
Uterine inversion.
In the UK database study, the major cause of PPH requiring massive transfusion was uterine atony (40%) and most of the women had been delivered via cesarean section (69%).
Subinvolution of placental site (most likely caused by an abnormal interaction between extravillous cytotrophoblasts and maternal uterine tissue).
Trauma.
Retained placental products (may be caused by tonic contractions of the uterus or abnormal placental implantation, such as placenta accreta, increta, or percreta).
Coagulation defects.
Active management of the third stage of labor consists of prophylactic uterotonics, uterine massage, and gentle cord traction. C
Active management of the third stage of labor is superior to expectant management for reducing PPH (NNT=12). A
Routine use of tranexamic acid to prevent PPH is not warranted. A
Active management of the third stage of labor is superior to expectant management for reducing PPH (NNT=12).
Authors of a Cochrane Review found reduced rates of mild and severe PPH, postpartum anemia, and need for transfusion with active management, but did not find cord drainage helpful in reducing PPH.

An overview of 29 systematic reviews found that active management of the third stage of labor as compared to expectant management using oxytocin or tranexamic acid significantly reduced postpartum hemorrhage >1000 mL; use of oral misoprostol or tranexamic acid reduced the number of blood transfusions.
Authors of a Cochrane review of three studies comparing IM and IV oxytocin found no difference in benefits (including PPH > 1000 mL) or risks.

One large RCT in 2018 demonstrated benefit of IV oxytocin over IM oxytocin in preventing severe PPH (5% vs. 8%) with a NNT to prevent one case of severe PPH of 29 (95% CI 16-201); however, there was no difference in the incidence of PPH of at least 500 mL.

Investigators conducting another RCT did not find a difference in major obstetric hemorrhage when given as a slow 5 IU bolus and infusion vs. infusion alone to otherwise healthy women after elective cesarean section; the addition of the bolus decreased the need for additional uterotonic agents.

In a small RCT of 51 women undergoing cesarean delivery, there were no differences in PPH between women who received a low-rate oxytocin infusion (16.7%) and those who received a high-rate infusion (15.4%).

Oral misoprostol was found in 2 studies to reduce PPH, but should be considered a second-line or third-line option. It is a reasonable choice in resource poor countries or for use during home births. In a quasi-experimental study of over 2,000 women, the incidence of PPH was 6.2% in the control group and 1.6% in the intervention group using a single misoprostol dose of 400 µg.

An RCT of 1721 women with expected vaginal deliveries at 36-42 weeks gestation was stopped early when interim analysis showed no benefit of misoprostol plus prophylactic oxytocin vs. oxytocin plus placebo on the rate of PPH (8.4% vs. 8,3%) while increasing adverse events (primarily fever and shivering).

In a Cochrane review of 11 trials of women undergoing cesarean deliveries, authors found that IV carbetocin (100 µg), a long-acting oxytocin agonist, reduced the need for therapeutic uterotonics compared with oxytocin but there was no difference in the incidence of PPH.

Analysis of over 39 trials found carbetocin, compared to oxytocin, reduced need for additional uterotonic use in women undergoing C-section and in high-risk women delivery vaginally. Additionally, the need for postpartum blood transfusion was decreased in high-risk women undergoing C-section.

IM carbetocin was noninferior to IM oxytocin in preventing PPH in a noninferiority trial including 29,645 women in 10 countries delivering vaginally. The frequency of blood loss of at least 500 ml or the use of additional uterotonic agents was 14.5% and 14.4%, respectively. There were no differences in rates of blood loss of at least 1000 ml which occurred in 1.51% in the carbetocin group and 1.45% in the oxytocin group.
An advantage of carbetocin is that it is heat stable and doesn’t require refrigeration as does oxytocin.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 papers found prophylactic intravenous tranexamic acid reduced total blood loss following cesarean section, and to a lesser extent after vaginal births, and may be helpful in reducing PPH; data are limited.

In a RCT of 4079 women of whom 3891 had a vaginal delivery, there was no significant difference in rate of PPH between those who received tranexamic acid and those given placebo (8.1% vs. 9.8%, respectively); this difference reflects a trend towards benefit (relative risk, 0.83; 95% CI 0.68 to 1.01; P=0.07).
A 2024 individual patient meta-analysis of more than 43,000 patients found a NNT of 500 to prevent 1 PPH, suggesting routine use of IV tranexamic acid is not warranted for routine prevention.
Refraining from unnecessary episiotomy will reduce the likelihood of PPH.

Studies are conflicting about whether or not uterine massage prevents PPH. Authors of a meta-analysis of three RCTs including 3842 women found no significant reduction in PPH comparing uterine massage, in addition to oxytocin and controlled cord traction to no uterine massage .
Delayed clamping of the umbilical cord (at least 30-60 seconds after birth) has advantages, particularly for preterm infants, and does not appear to increase the risk of PPH.

In a RCT in India, a protocol using misoprostol for secondary prevention in women with estimated postpartum bleeding ≥350 ml was noninferior to misoprostol as primary prevention with respect to PPH (<1% in both groups) or postpartum hemoglobin ≤7.8 g/dl (8.8% and 5.9%, respectively); only 92 women (4.2%) in the secondary prevention arm required misoprostol.
Immediate postpartum bimanual examination and visual inspection should be performed to evaluate for ongoing blood loss. C
Clinical estimation of blood loss is unreliable. C
Consider coagulation studies in selected patients. C
Immediate postpartum bimanual examination and visual inspection should be performed to evaluate for ongoing blood loss and its potential cause.
Clinical estimation of blood loss following either vaginal or operative delivery is unreliable as a diagnostic tool.
Using a pocket card containing images of blood on common obstetric materials increased accurate assessments of blood loss for all provider types across four of the six volumes tested.
Clinical signs include ongoing blood loss in the immediate postpartum period, low or decreased hemoglobin, and hypovolemic shock.
Clinical examination and transabdominal ultrasound is of limited usefulness in diagnosing the cause of secondary PPH.
Coagulation studies (platelets, international normalized ratio, partial thromboplastin time, and fibrinogen) may be beneficial in selected patients, especially those who are not forming clots.
A blood assay for the fibrin part of the clot based on thromboelastometry called fibtem A5 was found to be an independent predictor for progression to bleeds >2500 mL and of prolonged bleeding.
See for a management algorithm.

Key steps include appropriate resuscitation and treatment of any hemodynamic instability: uterotonics; straight catheterization of the urinary bladder; inspection for trauma with appropriate repair; evaluation for coagulopathies (especially in patients who are not forming clots); and manual removal of retained placenta.

Institution of a comprehensive management protocol across 29 delivery units resulted in a significant reduction in blood product use per 1000 births (−25.9%) at 10 months after implementation compared to before.

The protocol included algorithms for recognition of PPH based on vital signs and clinical suspicion; systematic use following vaginal birth of accessing help, fluid resuscitation, providing oxygen and uterine massage, emptying the bladder; use of intramuscular 0.2 mg methergine and 250 mcg hemabate, and rectal 800 to 1000 mcg cytotec for presumed uterine atony and an estimated blood loss over 1000 mL.

If bleeding continued, protocols included obtaining additional help, consideration of an operating room setting, obtaining additional intravenous access and laboratory tests, and use of appropriate procedures (e.g., D&C, uterine packing, and laceration repair).

For those with continued bleeding, estimated blood loss over 1500 mL, abnormal vital signs or coagulopathy, securing additional staff, use of transfusion and operative management as needed was outlined.
Consider uterine tamponade, uterine curettage, uterine artery embolization/ligation, or hysterectomy in cases of continued bleeding.
Uterotonics should be the first-line medical treatment in patients who have persistent hemorrhage after initial massage. A

Prophylactic oxytocin is the preferred uterotonic based on equal to superior efficacy and fewer side effects. Timing of administration of IV oxytocin before or after placental expulsion does not appear to be important with respect to PPH or other measured outcomes. A

Prostaglandins are effective in treating PPH, but are second-line or third-line options. The WHO has suggested using misoprostol as a first-line agent in resource-poor areas, but other studies have challenged this recommendation. B
Uterotonics should be the first-line medical treatment in patients who have persistent hemorrhage after initial massage.

Options include oxytocin 10 to 40 U/mL IV or 10 units IM; carbetocin 100 μg; methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM; prostaglandin (PG)F2-alpha 0.25 mg IM; misoprostol orally, sublingually, or rectally; and dinoprostone 20 mg suppository per vagina or per rectum.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 10 RCTs on treatment of primary PPH found few adequately powered trials. Oxytocin infusion is more effective than misoprostol and causes fewer side effects when used as first-line therapy for the treatment of primary PPH. When used after prophylactic uterotonics, misoprostol and oxytocin infusion work similarly.
Authors of two Cochrane reviews found decreased manual removal of the placenta and decreased side effects when comparing oxytocin alone with ergonovines or oxytocin/ergonovine combinations.
Adjunctive misoprostol with simultaneous administration of additional uterotonics does not appear to provide additional benefit for reducing maternal mortality or serious maternal morbidity.

In a RCT of 20,060 women with a clinical diagnosis of PPH after a vaginal birth or caesarean section enrolled from 193 hospitals in 21 countries, tranexamic acid vs. placebo given as a slow IV injection 1 to 3 hours following delivery (with a second dose, if needed) resulted in a small reduction in death from bleeding (1.5% vs. 1.9%; NNT 100) but no difference in the primary outcome of a composite of death from all causes or hysterectomy within 42 days of randomization.

An individual patient-level data meta-analysis of large RCTs confirmed benefit of tranexamic acid with increased overall survival from bleeding (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.08-1.33); benefit was greatest with immediate treatment which improved survival by more than 70%.
Repair of laceration(s) and/or rupture may be required.

Uterine curettage, uterine artery ligation, hypogastric artery ligation, hysterectomy, or angiographic embolization may be necessary if bleeding is not controlled. Risk factors predictive of the need for advanced interventional procedures in one study were abnormalities of placental implantation, prothrombin time <50% (or an International Normalized Ratio >1.64), fibrinogen <2 g/L, troponin detectable, and heart rate >115 bpm.

Bimanual uterine massage of the lower uterine segment for 10 minutes significantly reduced the rate of PPH (2.9% vs. 6.8% in the control group; relative risk 0.43, 95% CI, 0.21-0.90) in a RCT of 686 women from Thailand.

Authors of a systematic review of a heterogeneous group of low-quality RCTs in the setting of spontaneous vaginal delivery found that uterine massage in addition to IM oxytocin and controlled cord traction was not associated with a significantly lower risk of PPH (45/757 [5.9%] vs. 30/745 [4.0%], respectively) or differences in secondary outcomes.
Options include gauze packing, Foley balloon, and Sengstaken-Blakemore tube. Uterine balloon tamponade is discussed in detail elsewhere.
Authors of a systematic review found that uterine tamponade in resource-poor settings was an effective adjunctive treatment for PPH.

In a British population-based study of women requiring a second uterotonic agent, one quarter were managed with intrauterine tamponade prior to the use of a second-line agent; the success rate did not differ among women managed first with intrauterine tamponade. Uterine compression sutures were successful in 120 women (75% of those treated), pelvic vessel ligation was successful in five women (36% of those treated), interventional radiology was successful in 12 women (86% of those treated), and rFVIIa was successful in five women (31% of those treated)
A vacuum device performed well in a small case series of 10 women who failed first-line therapies for postpartum hemorrhage.

Two types of uterine compression sutures in association with intrauterine balloon tamponade were examined in a prospective observational study for women with pregnancies complicated by placenta previa and uterine atony; none of the women required hysterectomy.

In the British study noted above, uterine compression sutures were successful in 120 women (75% of those treated), pelvic vessel ligation was successful in five women (36% of those treated), interventional radiology was successful in 12 women (86% of those treated), and rFVIIa was successful in five women (31% of those treated).

A meta-analysis of 6 RCTs and 9 observational studies demonstrated uterine artery embolization for refractory PPH decreased volume of blood loss, operating time, and length of stay compared to hysterectomy.
Referral to a tertiary care facility is recommended in cases of suspected abnormal placentation.

Transfusion should be considered in patients who are hemodynamically unstable or for patients with a hemoglobin level of less than 9 g/dL who are actively bleeding; as no specific indications for transfusion exist, clinical judgment is paramount.

In an observational study, transfusion with whole blood resulted in fewer cases of renal tubular necrosis than use of packed red cells (0.3% vs. 2%); no other significant differences in outcomes were seen.

In a RCT of 521 women with anemia, defined as hemoglobin 4.8 to 7.9 g/dL (3.0-4.9 mmol/L) at 12 to 24 hours postpartum, but who were without severe symptoms, those who received a transfusion of packed red blood cells had only a small but not statistically significant difference in fatigue at 3 and 7 days compared to those randomized to non-intervention. There were no differences in health-related quality of life or physical complications.

Authors of a Cochrane review of management of postpartum anemia found one small RCT comparing erythropoietin to iron alone that demonstrated increased likelihood of lactation at hospital discharge (relative risk 1.90; 95% CI 1.21-2.98) but no apparent effect on need for blood transfusions. Additional studies are needed evaluating clinical outcomes.

In a population study of British women who required a second uterotonic agent, one quarter of women treated underwent hysterectomy as rescue therapy (2.2 cases per 10,000 women delivering [95% CI 1.9-2.5/10,000]).

The Shock Index (SI; heart rate/systolic blood pressure) obtained within the first hour of PPH of 1500 ml of blood or more, had a higher area under the curve (0.75) than these measures alone for predicting ICU admission. An SI <0.9 provides reassurance and an SI ≥1.7 indicates a need for urgent attention based on this study.

Investigators distributing questionnaires at 1 week and 2 and 4 months postpartum to a cohort of 206 women with primary PPH (defined as 1500 mL or more, and/or peripartum hemoglobin concentration fall to 7 g/dL or less) found 28% reported bleeding continuously for more than six weeks and 10% required hospital readmission within two months. Other mental and physical health outcomes appeared similar to general population reports with the exception of uterine infection (6% at 2 months).

In the WHO survey, 17.2% of the 352 reporting health facilities reported severe maternal outcomes following PPH; the incidence of these outcomes was associated with age, parity, gestational age, anemia, education, receipt of uterotonics for prophylaxis or treatment, referral from another facility, and Human Development Index group.

Among women who received uterine artery embolization, uterine devascularization, or uterine compression sutures for PPH, the vast majority (91.25%) of women resume normal menstruation within 6 months of delivery and most (77.87%) women who desire another pregnancy achieve conception based on a systematic review of 28 studies of outcomes after uterine artery embolization, uterine devascularization, or uterine compression sutures.
Monitor vital signs and hemoglobin levels until the patient is stable prior to discharge from hospital.

Prenatal vitamins and ferrous sulfate (equivalent to 120 mg elemental iron per day) are recommended to increase iron stores and replace red cell mass after PPH, if stable, or treat with packed red blood cells or intravenous iron if symptomatic and hemoglobin less than 7 g/dL
Some patients may benefit from stool softeners during iron therapy.
Obtain a hemoglobin level at 6 to 8 weeks postpartum.

cell.label: Active management of third stage of labor
Perform immediate postpartum bimanual examination and visual inspection to evaluate for ongoing blood loss and its potential cause.
Assess vital signs for hemodynamic compromise.
Perform bimanual uterine massage and assess its effect on uterine tone.
Give uterotonics and assess effect on uterine tone.
Perform visual inspection to evaluate for trauma.
Examine for any retained placental products via manual intrauterine examination or ultrasound (consider sedation prior to manual examination).
Evaluate for coagulopathies (consider especially in patients who are not forming clots).
Perform manual or surgical removal of retained placental products.
Appropriate resuscitative and stabilizing measures, including IVF and blood.
